one_liner: Single-header C++17 fast integer reader/writer for competitive programming: mmap plus 2-digit lookup tables, about 7-8x faster than std::cin.
what_it_does: fastio.hpp provides a global io object (and fastio::Reader, Writer, FastIO classes) with >>/<< operators, read<T>(), read(a,b,c), read_n(arr,n), readln, write_n, println and eof() for integers (including __int128), floats, chars and std::string. It is not an iostream drop-in, but FASTIO_REPLACE_CIN_COUT makes global cin/cout/endl alias io (no setw, fixed or tie). The repo also ships ten standalone headers (cin unsynced, scanf, getchar, getchar_unlocked, fread, streambuf, mmap variants) with the same interface for side-by-side comparison.
how_it_is_fast: For a regular file on stdin the Reader reserves an anonymous region, maps the file into it with MAP_FIXED|MAP_POPULATE and fills a trailing anonymous page with 0xFF sentinels, so the whitespace-skip and digit loops run without bounds checks. Integers are parsed two characters at a time through a 65536-entry uint16 table (v = v*100 + tbl[w] - 1) in a fixed unrolled sequence, with branchless sign handling and an optional 8-byte SWAR fold (FASTIO_SWAR8) for long 64-bit values. The Writer formats through a 10000-entry table of packed 4-digit ASCII words, computes 4-digit groups with independent constant divisions, stores them with one 16-byte SSE movups, and keeps a module-level fixed buffer with an index cursor so GCC keeps the cursor in a register; the hot path is forced always_inline.
when_to_use: Competitive programming or batch tools that read or write millions of decimal integers from redirected files (100 MiB of 9-digit ints: about 66-71 ms vs 490-565 ms for cin/ifstream)
Single-file submissions to online judges on Linux with GCC, where you can paste one header
Large integer output where cout or printf formatting dominates (about 94-155 ms vs 470 ms for cout on 100 MiB)
Input you control and can promise properties of (non-negative, fixed separators, known digit count) to unlock the compile-time fast options (reported 40% further on reads)
when_not_to_use: General file I/O, binary data or throughput-bound disk reads: the gain is decimal parsing and formatting, not faster I/O syscalls
Code that mixes this with scanf/cin on the same stream: the buffers do not see each other's consumed bytes
Interactive problems unless you flush after each round or build with FASTIO_STREAM; FASTIO_INPUT_MAX blocks until EOF
MSVC or non-GNU toolchains if you need __int128; Windows loses the mmap path (auto-disabled) and falls back to fread
Production code needing iostream formatting, locales, error reporting on malformed input, or a stable versioned API (3 stars, single author)

integration.dependencies: none (POSIX mmap/read on Unix; SSE intrinsics on x86 unless FASTIO_NO_WRITE_SSE)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; tested with g++ 14.2 -O2 (GCC-specific pragmas and always_inline; __int128 is a GNU extension)
integration.platforms: Linux/Unix with mmap for the fastest path; pipes, terminals and Windows fall back to read()/fread streaming; write SSE path is x86-only with a scalar fallback
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the global io object and module-level output buffer are shared state, so treat it as single-threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — FASTIO_REPLACE_CIN_COUT aliases global cin/cout/endl for >> and << on basic types, but iostream manipulators, tie, locales and error states are absent

gotchas: Compile-time options are promises about the data: FASTIO_INPUT_MAX silently drops input beyond the limit, FASTIO_OUTPUT_MAX overruns the heap buffer if exceeded, and FASTIO_NO_WS_SKIP or FASTIO_ASSUME_UNSIGNED produce wrong values on non-conforming input.
The author's own note says FASTIO_OUTPUT_MAX was once recommended for large output and was about 15% slower (24.5 MB output: 57 ms vs 49 ms streaming); keep it for tiny outputs only.
Buffered output is flushed by the destructor; _Exit() or a crash loses it, and reading -1 into an unsigned type is not treated specially.

The README's headline figures (69 ms / 132 ms), the benchvar table (70.7 / 155 ms), the benchlib table (66.5 / 94.3 ms) and the report.html table (65.3 / 123.6 ms) disagree; the author notes plus or minus 15% noise on a shared 2-core VM.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued filesystems-and-io siblings (liburing, SPDK, file_io_benchmark, fcp and the rest) parse text; pick fastio when the bottleneck is decimal integer parsing and formatting on stdin/stdout, and pick liburing or file_io_benchmark-style unbuffered reads when the bottleneck is raw bytes from storage.
verified_claims_summary: First-party runs on a shared 2-core Intel Xeon @2.60 GHz VM (model not stated), g++ 14.2 -O2, 100 MiB of about 9.98 million 9-digit integers in a warm /tmp file, median of 3 after a warm-up with checksums checked: read std::ifstream 489.6 ms vs fastio 66.5 ms (7.4x), write std::ofstream 469.5 ms vs 94.3 ms (5.0x) in make benchlib; make benchvar gives cin 565 ms vs 70.7 ms and cout 473 ms vs 155 ms. Unsyncing cin does not help here (578 ms), so the win is parsing and formatting, measured on page-cached data rather than disk I/O.
status_note: Actively developed by one author (last commit 2026-09-25, 3 stars, MIT, v1.3.0 features), with a CI workflow running self-tests and an 8 MiB quick benchmark; small enough to vendor as one header.
